analysis.title: Macro Picture: Peak Earnings
key_insights: US corporate profits hit a record share of GDP, the highest since WW2 on national accounts data. Tech and energy led, and the report argues earnings growth peaked in 2026.
Strong earnings let US equities reach record highs while PE multiples contracted, despite the Middle East conflict, a hawkish Fed under Warsh and multi-decade-high bond yields.
Tech accounts for about two-thirds of equal-weighted S&P 500 EPS growth in 2026 and energy for about a third. Tech's share is larger on a market-cap-weighted basis.
TS Lombard says the 1990s Greenspan-style hidden productivity boom does not apply today. NIPA profits match company-reported earnings, and profits are consistent with real unit labour costs.

Tech earnings are mostly recycled capex. More than 80% of AI-related revenues come from within the AI ecosystem, and hyperscaler capital gains on AI investments ('other income') also boosted 2026 tech earnings.
Puzzle 1: supercore inflation has stayed elevated while unit labour costs fell. Puzzle 2: r* estimates were revised up while the wage share fell to historical lows.
TS Lombard leans toward the hawkish resolution of both puzzles: wages reaccelerate, the labour share recovers, and corporate earnings slow in 2027.
Three drivers of slower 2027 earnings: the energy price boost fades, AI capex slows (consensus implies hyperscaler capex growth peaks now), and US growth shifts from productivity to hiring.
Because US consumers absorbed the energy shock by saving less, the household saving rate is likely to recover in 2027, which would reduce corporate earnings.
Labour demand is already reaccelerating and immigration controls limit supply, so capacity pressures and faster wage growth are expected.
TS Lombard views AI as labour-augmenting rather than labour-replacing. It expects AI gains to flow to workers and end users rather than raise the structural profit share.

On AI economics, TS Lombard leans toward the bearish commoditization thesis for datacenter owners and model developers. It points to $500bn of GPUs still to come online and Chinese open-weight models only 4-7 months behind the frontier.
The bull case for AI economics (Gavin Baker, Atreides) relies on Jevons paradox and NVIDIA acting as 'trainer of last resort'. TS Lombard doubts NVIDIA could backstop the labs in a supply glut.

sector_views.rationale: Tech earnings are mostly recycled hyperscaler capex and capital gains on AI cross-holdings. Slower capex and commoditization put these earnings at risk.
Energy contributed about a third of 2026 equal-weighted EPS growth, but the price impulse is expected to fade or at best stabilize in 2027.

earnings_insights: Equal-weighted S&P 500 EPS: tech explains about two-thirds of 2026 growth and energy about a third. This is a forward 12-month estimate series from Bloomberg.
NIPA corporate profits rose 25% y/y in 2026Q2 (reported official data), with tech and energy leading.
PE multiples contracted in 2026 even as stocks hit record highs, because earnings rose faster than prices.
TS Lombard expects slower US earnings growth in 2027 (house forecast, not consensus).

macro_indicators.interpretation: Profits as a share of GDP are at a record, the highest since WW2.

macro_indicators.indicator: Recycled capex share of AI ecosystem revenues
macro_indicators.interpretation: TS Lombard's own estimate. Most AI revenue comes from other AI ecosystem spending, not outside customers.
Slowing capex growth would reverse the recycled-revenue dynamics that boosted tech earnings.
This spending is the main source of tech sector revenue and earnings.
The house view is that wages accelerate and the profit share declines.

risk_factors: Energy prices fall if the Middle East crisis is resolved, reversing the 2026 profit boost.
Hyperscaler AI capex slows and tech valuations drop, removing 'paper earnings' and capital gains on AI cross-holdings.
Household saving rate recovers in 2027 and reduces corporate earnings.
Labour market tightens, wages accelerate and the labour share rises.
A glut of GPU supply, with $500bn still to come online, could push rental prices down and cause datacenter bankruptcies.
Chinese open-weight models eroding the moats of the frontier US labs.

tension_points.bull_case: Jevons paradox: falling token prices trigger demand growth, keeping GPU rentals high and datacenters profitable. NVIDIA acts as trainer of last resort (Gavin Baker, Atreides).
tension_points.bear_case: Commoditization: $500bn of GPUs still to come online and Chinese open-weight models only 4-7 months behind lead to a race to the bottom (Harris Kupperman, Praetorian Capital, and TS Lombard's lean).
tension_points.what_invalidates: Large rise in consumer and business AI subscriptions from outside the AI ecosystem, and GPU rental prices staying high as new supply arrives.

tension_points.bull_case: AI bulls compare 2026 to the mid-1990s, when earnings surprises signalled a hidden productivity boom that raised profits.
tension_points.bear_case: Energy impulse fades, AI capex slows, wages reaccelerate and the profit share declines, as the profit share fell in the late 1990s.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that a larger share of AI revenues comes from outside the AI ecosystem, from consumers and non-tech businesses finding genuine productivity gains.

theme_stances.key_argument: Earnings growth may have peaked as energy support fades, AI capex slows and wages accelerate.
theme_stances.evidence: Our view that US wages will accelerate and productivity slow is obviously not the market consensus.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI will eventually be commoditized for both datacenter owners and model developers, with benefits flowing to end users.
theme_stances.evidence: We lean towards the more bearish thesis and the idea that AI will eventually be commoditized
